extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent prosecutors and practitioners (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 using a two-step analysis (statutory category + judicial exceptions), with factors and examples for product and process claims, especially computer-implemented and biotech-related claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step subject matter eligibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two criteria for determining subject matter eligibility and both must be satisfied. The claimed invention (1) must be directed to one of the four statutory categories, and (2) must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two-step analysis: Step 1 — Is the claim directed to process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter? Step 2 — Does the claim wholly embrace a judicial exception (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas), or is it a particular practical application of an exception? Conduct both steps during examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four categories of statutory subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to one of the four patent-eligible subject matter categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions as articulated by courts: Process = an act or series of acts or steps; Machine = a concrete thing consisting of parts or combination of devices; Manufacture = an article produced from materials by giving new forms/qualities; Composition of matter = compositions of two or more substances or composite articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory examples (claims not within the four categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to one of the statutory categories include transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., propagating electrical/electromagnetic signal per se), a naturally occurring organism, a human per se, a legal contractual agreement, a game defined as a set of rules, a computer program per se, a company, and a mere arrangement of printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four categories, it is not patent eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 for that reason. Provide examples and cite relevant case law (In re Nuijten, Chakrabarty, Gottschalk v. Benson, In re Miller, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that encompass both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (under the broadest reasonable interpretation) embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim's broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification encompasses non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable media that includes a carrier wave), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is appropriate. If amendment could cure the defect, still conduct Step 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicially recognized exceptions include laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas. A claim wholly directed to such an exception is not eligible for patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim is for a particular practical application of the exception (which may be eligible) or whether it claims the exception itself (which is ineligible). Consider other descriptive terms used in precedent (natural phenomena, scientific principles, mental processes, disembodied mathematical algorithms), and consult case law (Bilski, Diehr, Chakrabarty, Funk Bros., Le Roy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is limited to a particular practical application of a judicial exception is eligible for patent protection; a claim that is directed to the abstract idea, law of nature, or physical phenomenon itself is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the claim, as a whole, is for a particular practical application having a real world use. Practical application is shown when an abstract idea or law of nature is applied to a tangible structure or process in a way that does not preempt substantially all uses of the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application for product claims (machines, manufactures, compositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For product categories, eligible items are non-naturally occurring products typically formed of tangible elements or parts that embody a particular or specific, tangible practical application of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product claims that recite tangible structural limitations (e.g., 'a machine comprising...') are more likely to show a practical application. Claims that recite product categories but lack tangible limitations (i.e., cover every way of applying an abstract concept) are not limited to a practical application and are ineligible. Evaluate whether the claim's limitations limit the claim to a tangible embodiment and whether preemption of other applications occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application for process (method) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim must be limited to a particular practical application to be statutory under 35 U.S.C. 101; not every claimed method qualifies as a statutory process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inquiries and factors (including the machine-or-transformation test as a useful investigative tool) to determine whether the method claim is directed to an abstract idea or is a patent-eligible practical application. Consider whether recited steps are merely field-of-use or insignificant post-solution activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test (investigative tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue for determining whether a claimed invention is a process under § 101: (1) tied to a particular machine/apparatus, or (2) transforms a particular article into a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not the sole test, use it as part of the fact-specific analysis. Passing the test supports eligibility; failing it does not automatically render a claim ineligible, but it is relevant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor: particularity or generality of machine elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a machine or apparatus is recited, consider the degree to which the machine in the claim can be specifically identified (the particularity of the machine elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporation of a particular, well-defined machine or apparatus into the claimed method weighs toward eligibility. Broad recitation of 'a computer' without particularized structure may be insufficient unless programming specifics make it a special-purpose computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor: whether the machine/apparatus implements the steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the recited machine/apparatus actually implements the steps of the method (integral to performance) or is merely an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral use of the machine to perform the method steps weighs toward eligibility. A machine that cannot perform the claimed steps (e.g., Internet merely as data source) or is only tangentially involved weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor: extrasolution activity and field-of-use limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the machine's involvement or other recited activity is insignificant 'extra-solution' activity or merely a field-of-use limitation that does not meaningfully limit the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field-of-use limitations and insignificant activities (e.g., mere data-gathering that all applications of the method would require) do not impose meaningful limits and weigh against eligibility. Cite examples (Bilski, Parker v. Flook, Cybersource).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented process requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented processes, a general purpose computer may be sufficiently particular when programmed to perform the claimed steps (programming creates a new, special-purpose machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must clearly convey that the computer is programmed to perform the method steps; mere addition of 'computer-aided' or performing on a computer, without explanation of how the computer aids or the significance of the computer, is insufficient to render an abstract concept patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-readable medium (manufacture) guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-transitory, tangible computer-readable storage medium that possesses structural limitations qualifies as a manufacture and would be patent-eligible subject matter if the claim as a whole has a real-world use and does not cover substantially all practical uses of a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding executable instructions or stored data to such a statutory-eligible medium does not render it non-statutory so long as the claim as a whole remains a tangible embodiment and practical application. Evaluate whether claim still impermissibly preempts all uses of an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption as a central concern
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim impermissibly covers substantially all practical applications of a judicial exception (preempts the exception), it is not patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim's breadth would grant a monopoly over the basic tools of scientific and technological work. Use examples (e.g., hedging in Bilski) to illustrate preemption concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to be weighed (favorable vs unfavorable) in abstract-idea determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that weigh in favor of patent-eligibility satisfy the machine-or-transformation test or provide evidence that the abstract idea has been practically applied; factors that weigh against do neither.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple, non-exclusive factors in each case; do not reach a conclusion based on a single factor while ignoring others. Anticipate development of new factors for emerging technologies and update analysis with new precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 (what examiner must state)
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a rejection for failure to claim patent-eligible subject matter, identify the natural principle/abstract idea, identify that the claim is effectively directed to that principle, and explain reasons the additional claim features or combination of features fail to integrate the principle into a practical application or fail to be sufficient to amount to significantly more than the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear analysis showing which inquiry the claim fails (e.g., passes Inquiries 1-2 but fails Inquiry 3) and why. Use sample rejections (e.g., insulin dosage example) as models for structure and required explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating applicant responses and permissible amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper response to a subject-matter-eligibility rejection is an amendment adding features or amending existing features that integrate the judicial exception into the process (practically apply it) and are sufficient to limit the application to more than the principle itself, or persuasive argument that the additional steps add something significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of persuasive amendments: add non-conventional, non-routine steps; claim a device that integrates the principle (e.g., a sanitizing device using UV light with specific structure) rather than merely instructing to 'apply' the principle. A showing that steps are not routine, well-known, or conventional can be persuasive. Refer to 2012 Interim Guidance for additional examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant post-solution activity and field-of-use limitations are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that are mere fields of use or insignificant post-solution activity do not render an otherwise abstract claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding steps that simply confine an abstract idea to a particular environment (e.g., 'for use with a machine') or adding data-gathering steps that are routine will not save a claim. Cite Parker v. Flook and Bilski decisions and relevant examples in the MPEP.
